phonemes.desc: Aspirated theta [tʰ], the breathy initial consonant.
Long eta [ɛː], the first syllable's length.
Short iota with acute plus alpha — the pitch peak on the second syllable.

pronunciation.approximation: 'thay-EE-ah' — the first syllable is long and level, the second pitched high and bright.

kin.label: Greek
kin.form: Θεία (Theía), Titaness of sight, shining, and the bright upper air

kin.label: Root
kin.form: θέα (théa), 'sight, view'; related to θεάομαι, 'to gaze'

kin.label: Children
kin.form: Hēlios, Selēnē, and Eōs — sun, moon, and dawn

pronunciation.note: Theía is Tier 1 because the Greek Θεία contains both length (η in the first syllable) and stress (acute on the ι of the second). She is the Titaness whose children are the celestial lights.

domains.title: Titaness of Sight and Light
domains.subtitle: Brilliance, The Eyes, The Celestial Luminaries
domains.lead: Theía is the Titaness of sight, shining, and the bright ether. Though less famous than her children Hēlios, Selēnē, and Eōs, she is the luminous source from which they spring — the divine principle that makes seeing and being seen possible.

cards.name: Mother of Lights
cards.desc: By Hyperion she bore the sun, moon, and dawn — the three great celestial bodies.

cards.name: Goddess of Sight
cards.desc: Her name links her to θέα, 'sight'; she is the power behind clear vision.

cards.name: Shining Ether
cards.desc: She personifies the bright upper air through which light travels.

cards.name: Titanic Lineage
cards.desc: Daughter of Ouranos and Gē, sister of Kronos and Rhea, aunt of Zeus.

symbols.name: Radiant eyes
symbols.meaning: The organs of sight over which she presides

symbols.name: Bright ether or aithēr
symbols.meaning: The luminous medium of the upper sky

symbols.name: Gold and clear crystal
symbols.meaning: Materials that catch and transmit light

mythology.lead: Theía has no independent narrative myths; her importance is genealogical and cosmological. Through her, the Titans bequeath light to the Olympian cosmos.

myths.title: Birth of the Luminaries
myths.text: Hesiod names Theía as the wife of Hyperion and mother of Hēlios (Sun), Selēnē (Moon), and Eōs (Dawn). The trio governs the visible heavens; without Theía, there is no source from which these lights can arise.

myths.title: Theía in Thessaly
myths.text: Pausanias mentions a sanctuary of Theía in Thessaly, where she was honored as mother of the sun. Her cult was local and relatively rare, overshadowed by the greater worship of her children.

myths.title: Sight and Divinity
myths.text: The name Theía is related to Greek words for sight and wonder; some ancient sources connected it with θεός, 'god,' via the idea that the divine is what is seen or what shines forth. The etymology is linguistically uncertain but poetically suggestive.

lore.syncretism: Theía was sometimes identified with Aphrodite in her celestial aspect, since both were associated with shining and with the planet Venus. In Orphic cosmogonies she appears among the primordial generations, often linked with light and vision. Her children absorbed most of her functions: Helios as sun, Selene as moon, Eos as dawn. Roman poets mention her as Theia but did not develop a distinct cult.
lore.culturalLegacy: Theía survives chiefly in her children and in the vocabulary of vision. Words derived from her root — theory, theater, theorem — preserve the Greek sense that seeing is knowing. In astronomy, her name has been given to a hypothesized proto-planet that collided with early Earth and formed the Moon, a modern scientific tribute to the Titaness of light.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Theía is the unseen source of all that is seen. She has no myths because her power is too basic for narrative: it is the condition under which any story can be witnessed. To honor her is to recognize that light is not merely physical but epistemic — we know by seeing, and we are known by being seen.

Her restoration in Unicode is fitting. The very act of reading a restored Greek name on a screen depends on light, on sight, on the luminous technology that her children prefigured. Theía reminds us that behind every visible marvel there is an older, quieter power: the brightness that makes brightness possible.
lore.archaeology: Theía had no Panhellenic sanctuary of note. A local cult in Thessaly is mentioned by Pausanias, and she appears in the genealogical poetry of Hesiod and the Orphic tradition. Her iconographic presence is largely indirect: she is implied by the numerous representations of her children Helios, Selene, and Eos in Greek and Roman art.
